questions.stem: A 44 year old lone father has an 8 month history of constant worry about his children, his job and money. He cannot switch the worry off, feels tense and irritable, and struggles to concentrate at work. His mood is otherwise normal and he still enjoys football. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Excessive, uncontrollable worry across several everyday domains for at least 6 months with tension, irritability and poor concentration is GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: his children, his job and money
steps.x: Uncontrollable worry about **many** areas for **more than 6 months**, with normal mood.

elim: Begins within weeks of a stressor and settles; his worry is about many areas for 8 months.
His mood and enjoyment are preserved.
Needs intrusive obsessions and compulsions, not everyday worry.
Fear is specific to social situations.

steps.x: **C. Generalised anxiety disorder.** Multi-domain uncontrollable worry for 6+ months = GAD.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has a 3 month history of worrying about her health, her husband's job and her children's schooling. She finds it hard to control and feels tense and tired. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Thyroid function and full blood count are normal. Her GP is considering generalised anxiety disorder.
questions.q: Which additional feature is required to make this diagnosis?
o: A panic attack in the past month
Symptoms present for at least 2 weeks
Symptoms present for at least 6 months
questions.e: GAD requires excessive, uncontrollable worry about several areas for at least 6 months causing distress or impairment.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional feature is required to make this diagnosis?
Everything fits except the **time course**.

elim: Panic attacks are not required for GAD.
Two weeks is the depression threshold; GAD needs 6 months.

steps.x: **E. Symptoms present for at least 6 months.** GAD needs 6 months of worry.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with an 11 month history of worry about many things is assessed in a mental health clinic. When asked how he slept last night, he describes the drive home, his dinner and a phone call in detail before finally answering that he slept badly. He does return to the question. His pulse rate is 90 bpm.
questions.q: Which term best describes his speech?
questions.e: Circumstantiality, with excessive detail before eventually reaching the point, is a recognised feature of GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which term best describes his speech?

clues: He does return to the question
steps.x: Lots of detail but he **gets there in the end**.

elim: Rapid jumps between loosely linked ideas, seen in mania.
Illogical leaps between unrelated ideas, seen in schizophrenia.
Repeating the same answer or idea.
Wanders off and never returns to the point.

steps.x: **A. Circumstantiality.** Circumstantial = gets to the point; tangential = never does.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 9 month history of uncontrollable worry about her family and finances. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. Thyroid function tests are normal. She is examined by her GP.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands
questions.e: Chronic sympathetic activation in GAD causes tremor, sweating and palpitations.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: uncontrollable worry about her family and finances
steps.x: GAD with the thyroid **excluded**: look for the sympathetic sign.

elim: Suggests thyroid disease; her thyroid tests are normal.
A sign of hyperthyroidism, which has been excluded.

steps.x: **A. Fine tremor of the outstretched hands.** GAD physical signs: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, muscle tension.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder has noticed his heart 'pounding' during periods of worry. He has no chest pain, breathlessness or blackouts. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and regular and BP 128/80 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is recorded. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Normal sinus rhythm at 88 bpm with no ST or T wave change.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the ECG?
o: ST depression in the lateral leads
questions.e: The ECG in GAD is typically normal; palpitations reflect awareness of sympathetic drive.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on the ECG?

clues: no chest pain, breathlessness or blackouts
steps.x: Regular pulse at 88 with anxiety-linked palpitations.

elim: No reason for it and it does not cause pounding.
No chest pain; ischaemia is not suggested.

steps.x: **C. Normal sinus rhythm.** GAD: ECG typically normal.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder is brought to the Emergency Department breathing fast and feeling terrified after an argument. She has tingling around her mouth. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 100% breathing air. An arterial blood gas is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the arterial blood gas?
questions.e: A panic attack drives hyperventilation, blowing off CO2 and causing an acute respiratory alkalosis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on the arterial blood gas?
Hyperventilation **blows off CO2**.

elim: Compensated respiratory acidosis, as in COPD.

steps.x: **D. Raised pH with low PaCO2.** Panic attack: high pH, low PaCO2 = respiratory alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder has had four episodes in 2 months of sudden breathlessness, palpitations and an intense fear that she is about to die. Each peaks within 10 minutes and settles within half an hour. Between episodes she worries that another will happen. ECG and troponin during an episode were normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of these episodes?
questions.e: Recurrent sudden episodes of breathlessness, palpitations and intense fear of dying are panic attacks, which commonly accompany GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of these episodes?

clues: sudden breathlessness, palpitations and an intense fear that she is about to die
ECG and troponin during an episode were normal
steps.x: Sudden, brief, fear-driven episodes with normal tests.

elim: ECG and troponin were normal, and she is young.
The ECG during an episode was normal.
Rare; episodes with hypertension and headache, not driven by fear.
Does not recur briefly and settle in 30 minutes.

steps.x: **B. Panic attacks.** Recurrent panic attacks = panic disorder, often alongside GAD.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has had generalised anxiety disorder for 4 years and has declined treatment. He now drinks 6 cans of strong lager each evening because it 'stops the worrying'. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 142/90 mmHg. Investigations show a raised gamma-GT and MCV.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication of his anxiety?
questions.e: Untreated GAD can lead to substance misuse as self-medication, alongside depression and functional impairment.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely complication of his anxiety?
He is **self-medicating** with alcohol.

elim: Not a complication of anxiety; macrocytosis and gamma-GT point to alcohol.

steps.x: **A. Alcohol misuse.** GAD complications: depression, substance misuse, impairment, sleep problems.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has a 7 month history of worry about many aspects of her life. She has asthma, works as a teacher and is vegetarian. Her mother and sister have both been treated for anxiety. She had a depressive episode at university. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature of her history most increases her risk of generalised anxiety disorder?
o: Family history of anxiety and previous depression
questions.e: Family history and previous anxiety or depression are recognised risk factors for GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which feature of her history most increases her risk of generalised anxiety disorder?

clues: Her mother and sister have both been treated for anxiety
steps.x: Look for **family history** and **previous mental illness**.

elim: Mild asthma is not the key risk here.
The peak risk age is 35 to 54.
Occupation is not a recognised risk factor.

steps.x: **C. Family history of anxiety and previous depression.** GAD risk: family history, previous anxiety/depression, chronic illness, age 35 to 54, living alone.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman is referred to cardiology with a year of palpitations and sweating. A 48-hour Holter shows sinus rhythm throughout and thyroid function is normal. She says she worries constantly about her job, her parents' health and her son's exams and cannot stop. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Somatic symptoms of sympathetic activation with a normal heart rhythm, normal thyroid and multi-domain uncontrollable worry is GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: worries constantly about her job, her parents' health and her son's exams
steps.x: Physical symptoms with **normal** tests, plus constant worry.

elim: The Holter showed sinus rhythm throughout.
Hot flushes and menstrual change would be expected; the worry is the key feature.
Rare, with paroxysmal hypertension and headache.

steps.x: **A. Generalised anxiety disorder.** Physical symptoms with normal tests and worry about everything = GAD.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has a 10 month history of uncontrollable worry about work, money and his health. He feels restless and keyed up most days. His mood is normal. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. He complains that his sleep is poor.
questions.q: Which sleep pattern is most likely?
o: Difficulty falling asleep because of worrying
Excessive daytime sleep with normal nights
Reduced need for sleep without tiredness
Waking 2 hours early with low mood
questions.e: Sleep disturbance in GAD is usually difficulty getting to sleep as worries keep going round.

steps.x: The question asks: which sleep pattern is most likely?
Normal mood, constant worry.

elim: Early morning waking is typical of depression.

steps.x: **A. Difficulty falling asleep because of worrying.** GAD = initial insomnia; depression = early morning waking.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman who separated from her husband a year ago and now lives alone has a 9 month history of worrying about everything. She describes herself as 'a born worrier'. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. Investigations are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Age 35 to 54, separation and living alone are risk factors; generalised worry for over 6 months is GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Risk factors plus **generalised** worry for months.

elim: Needs a trauma with flashbacks and avoidance.

steps.x: **B. Generalised anxiety disorder.** GAD risk profile: 35 to 54, separated, living alone, lone parent.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 7 month history of worry, restlessness and palpitations. She has also lost 4 kg, prefers cold rooms and has loose stools. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 132/70 mmHg. Her GP thinks she may have generalised anxiety disorder but wants to exclude its most important mimic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Hyperthyroidism is the key mimic of GAD; weight loss, heat intolerance and loose stools make TFTs essential.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Anxiety **plus** weight loss and heat intolerance.

elim: Phaeochromocytoma is rare and not the first test.
Cushing's does not give this picture.

steps.x: **D. Thyroid function tests.** Always check TFTs before diagnosing GAD.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has a 10 month history of excessive worry about many things, muscle tension and poor sleep. Baseline blood tests are normal. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. A junior doctor asks which test will confirm generalised anxiety disorder.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Clinical assessment of history and mental state
questions.e: GAD is diagnosed by clinical assessment; tests only exclude contributors.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
Tests are normal: no test confirms GAD.
**A. Clinical assessment of history and mental state.** GAD is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 7 month history of worry, fatigue and poor concentration. She also feels breathless climbing stairs and has very heavy periods. She looks pale. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Thyroid function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Baseline tests in GAD include FBC to exclude anaemia, which can add to fatigue and palpitations.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Pale, menorrhagia, breathless: **anaemia** as a contributor.

elim: No respiratory features to suggest it.
Breathlessness here is likely from anaemia.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count.** GAD baseline: FBC, TFTs, glucose, U&Es.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man is being assessed for generalised anxiety disorder after a year of worry, sweating and shakiness. He also reports thirst, passing urine often at night and blurred vision. His BMI is 34 kg/m2. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. Thyroid function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Baseline bloods for GAD include glucose to exclude diabetes as a contributor; thirst, nocturia and obesity make it important here.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next investigation?

clues: thirst, passing urine often at night
steps.x: Osmotic symptoms in an obese man.

elim: Hypercalcaemia can cause thirst but diabetes is far more likely here.
For diabetes insipidus, which is rare.

steps.x: **A. Blood glucose.** Baseline bloods exclude anaemia, thyroid disease and diabetes.

questions.stem: A GP is reviewing five patients with generalised anxiety disorder who all mention palpitations. Their thyroid tests and resting ECGs are normal. She wants to choose the patient in whom a 24 to 48 hour ambulatory ECG is most clearly warranted.
questions.q: In which patient is ambulatory ECG monitoring most warranted?
o: New palpitations during exercise with a near-faint
Palpitations that settle with slow breathing
questions.e: New-onset palpitations, especially exercise-induced or with syncope or near-syncope, warrant a 24 or 48-hour Holter.

steps.x: The question asks: in which patient is ambulatory ECG monitoring most warranted?
Look for the **red flags**: exertion and near-syncope.

elim: Typical of anxiety and not new.

steps.x: **B. New palpitations during exercise with a near-faint.** Exertional palpitations or (near-)syncope = Holter.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has just been diagnosed with mild generalised anxiety disorder after 7 months of worry. He is working and has no suicidal thoughts. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. He asks what happens next.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Education about anxiety and guided self-help
questions.e: NICE CG113 starts with education and reassurance, then low-intensity psychological interventions such as guided self-help.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial management?
Mild GAD: start at the **bottom of the stepped care** ladder.

elim: Benzodiazepines are not first-line and cause dependence.
Treats only somatic symptoms; not the first step.
Drugs are second-line or for severe GAD.

steps.x: **B. Education about anxiety and guided self-help.** Step 1: education; step 2: low-intensity interventions.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with mild generalised anxiety disorder has been given information about anxiety. Her GP wants to offer a low-intensity psychological intervention, as recommended by NICE. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is a low-intensity psychological intervention?
questions.e: Low-intensity interventions are psychoeducation, individual self-guided help and psychoeducational groups.

steps.x: The question asks: which is a low-intensity psychological intervention?
Low-intensity = education, self-help, groups.

elim: Not a low-intensity intervention for GAD.

steps.x: **E. Psychoeducational group.** Low intensity: self-help and psychoeducational groups.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder has completed 8 weeks of guided self-help with little change. His symptoms now interfere with his work. He does not want to take medication. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: After failed low-intensity input, step up to high-intensity CBT or sertraline; CBT is the most important psychological treatment.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: does not want to take medication
steps.x: Step up, and respect his **preference**.

elim: Avoid benzodiazepines; and he does not want medication.
He does not want medication; high-intensity therapy is equally appropriate.

steps.x: **B. Individual high-intensity CBT.** Step 3: high-intensity CBT or sertraline.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with severe generalised anxiety disorder is starting sertraline. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. She has no thoughts of self-harm. She asks how long it will be before she notices a benefit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: 2 to 4 weeks, and anxiety may worsen at first
Within 1 hour of the first dose
questions.e: Sertraline takes 2 to 4 weeks to work and can initially make anxiety worse.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate advice?
SSRIs are slow, and can make things worse first.
**C. 2 to 4 weeks, and anxiety may worsen at first.** Sertraline: 2 to 4 weeks, warn about early worsening.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with severe generalised anxiety disorder starts sertraline 50 mg daily. He has no history of self-harm. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg. The GP plans his follow-up.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate follow-up plan?
o: Review at 1 week, then as needed
Review every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months
Review only if side effects occur
questions.e: Over 30s are reviewed every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months; under 30s are seen at 1 week.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate follow-up plan?
His **age** decides the plan.

elim: The 1-week review is for those under 30.

steps.x: **C. Review every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months.** Sertraline follow-up: under 30 at 1 week; over 30 every 2 to 4 weeks for 3 months.

questions.stem: A 35 year old violinist with generalised anxiety disorder is doing well with CBT. Her worry is improving, but before concerts her heart races and her hands shake, which affects her playing. She has no asthma. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Beta-blockers treat somatic symptoms such as racing heart and tremor, but not the central worry.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate additional treatment?

clues: heart races and her hands shake
steps.x: **Somatic** symptoms only; worry is improving.

elim: Used for GAD when SSRIs and SNRIs are unsuitable, not for performance tremor.

steps.x: **D. Propranolol.** Beta-blockers for somatic symptoms; they do not treat worry.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder asks his GP for a regular prescription of diazepam because a friend's tablets 'calmed him right down'. He has not tried any treatment. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain long-term benzodiazepines cause dependence and offer stepped care
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily
questions.e: Benzodiazepines should be avoided long-term because of dependence and rebound anxiety; offer education, psychological therapy and SSRIs.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate response?
A request for **long-term** benzodiazepine.

elim: Long-term use causes tolerance and dependence.
Also causes dependence and does not treat GAD.

steps.x: **A. Explain long-term benzodiazepines cause dependence and offer stepped care.** Avoid long-term benzodiazepines in GAD.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder is reviewed 2 weeks after starting sertraline. She says she has been thinking for a week that her family would be better off without her and has looked up ways to end her life. She has stopped going to work. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase sertraline and review in 4 weeks
Stop sertraline and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Persistent suicidal ideation or severe functional impairment needs assessment and urgent mental health review.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: looked up ways to end her life
steps.x: Persistent ideation with planning.

elim: Too slow for persistent suicidal ideation.
Inadequate for this level of risk.

steps.x: **E. Urgent mental health review.** Suicidal ideation in GAD = urgent mental health review.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder has recurrent sudden episodes of palpitations, breathlessness and fear of dying, and now avoids the supermarket in case one happens. Cardiac tests are normal. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She is diagnosed with panic disorder.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her panic disorder?
questions.e: Panic disorder, like GAD, is treated first-line with CBT.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her panic disorder?
Panic disorder first-line is psychological.

elim: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for panic disorder.
Not a treatment and can be unsafe.

steps.x: **B. Cognitive behavioural therapy.** Panic disorder: CBT first-line.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man with severe generalised anxiety disorder has taken sertraline, then escitalopram, each at a full dose for 10 weeks, with little benefit. He is not suicidal. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. He wants to try another medication.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication?
questions.e: If sertraline fails or is not tolerated, try another SSRI or an SNRI such as venlafaxine or duloxetine.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate medication?
Two SSRIs have failed.
**C. Duloxetine.** After SSRI failure: an SNRI (venlafaxine or duloxetine).

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder asks why her brain 'won't stop worrying'. She has a 9 month history of worry about many things. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm. Her psychiatrist explains the current model of the condition.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying mechanism?
o: Dopamine excess in the mesolimbic pathway
Dysregulated serotonin, noradrenaline and GABA in the amygdala and prefrontal cortex
Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra
questions.e: GAD reflects dysregulation of serotonin, noradrenaline and GABA in the amygdala and prefrontal cortex, with heightened threat perception and impaired regulation of worry.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely underlying mechanism?
Think of the **threat circuit** and its neurotransmitters.
**B. Dysregulated serotonin, noradrenaline and GABA in the amygdala and prefrontal cortex.** GAD: amygdala and PFC, with 5-HT, NA and GABA dysregulation.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder has muscle aches in his neck and shoulders, a fine tremor and sweaty palms. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. Thyroid function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his physical symptoms?
questions.e: Chronic sympathetic activation causes muscle tension, tremor, palpitations and sweating in GAD.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of his physical symptoms?
Tremor, sweating, tachycardia, tension: the **fight or flight** system.

elim: Would cause cramps and tingling, not sweating and tachycardia.
Causes numbness, not sweating and tremor.

steps.x: **A. Chronic sympathetic activation.** GAD somatic symptoms = chronic sympathetic activation.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder has a panic attack in clinic. She is breathing rapidly and complains of tingling in her fingers and around her lips. Her total serum calcium taken an hour ago was normal. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her tingling?
o: Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin
Excess calcium excretion by the kidneys
questions.e: Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, which increases calcium binding to albumin and lowers the ionised fraction, causing perioral and peripheral paraesthesia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of her tingling?

clues: tingling in her fingers and around her lips
total serum calcium taken an hour ago was normal
steps.x: Total calcium normal, but the **free** fraction falls.

elim: Too slow; this is an acute change in binding.

steps.x: **A. Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin.** Respiratory alkalosis -> more Ca bound to albumin -> low ionised Ca -> tingling.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with severe generalised anxiety disorder has taken sertraline for 4 days. He is disappointed that he feels no better, though blood levels of the drug are expected to be steady within a week. His pulse rate is 90 bpm.
questions.q: Which best explains why the benefit takes weeks to appear?
o: Slow conversion to an active prodrug
Slow penetration of the blood-brain barrier
questions.e: SSRIs raise synaptic serotonin quickly, but the anxiolytic benefit depends on gradual downregulation of anxiety-related limbic hyperactivity over weeks.

steps.x: The question asks: which best explains why the benefit takes weeks to appear?

clues: blood levels of the drug are expected to be steady within a week
steps.x: The drug is there, but the **brain adaptation** is slow.

elim: Not the reason for delayed effect.

steps.x: **B. Gradual downregulation of limbic hyperactivity.** SSRI benefit lags because limbic adaptation takes weeks.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder takes propranolol. His racing heart and tremor have settled, but he still worries constantly about his work and family. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which best explains why his worry has not improved?
o: He has developed tolerance to propranolol
Propranolol blocks peripheral beta receptors and does not treat central cognitive symptoms
The dose is too low to block beta receptors
questions.e: Beta-blockers reduce peripheral beta-adrenergic activation (tachycardia, tremor) but do not address the central cognitive component.

steps.x: The question asks: which best explains why his worry has not improved?

clues: racing heart and tremor have settled
steps.x: Body symptoms better, mind unchanged.

elim: His pulse rate of 64 shows effective beta-blockade.

steps.x: **C. Propranolol blocks peripheral beta receptors and does not treat central cognitive symptoms.** Beta-blockers treat the body, not the worry.
